title: Mount a shaft between bench centres: hold the tailstock lever down, seat one end, let the sprung centre in
instruction: Mount the shaft between the centres: hold the lever down, seat one end on the fixed point, swing it in line, ease the lever up.
context: Turned shafts, spindles and pins are checked for runout by mounting them between the 60-degree points of a bench centre and turning them under a dial indicator; inspectors, and machinists checking their own parts, do this for first-article and lot-sample checks every shift. The left point is fixed; the right one is on a sprung sleeve that a hand lever draws back. One hand holds the lever down while the other sets one centre hole on the fixed point and swings the shaft into line; the lever is then eased up so the sprung point enters the other hole. A point riding on the chamfer instead of its seat reads a false runout, and a dropped shaft is scrap. Done by: inspectors, testers, sorters, samplers and weighers (O*NET 51-9061.00, 602,000 US jobs, 2025): "Position products, components, or parts for testing"; machinists (51-4041.00, 288,300 US jobs, 2025).
setup:
Millimetres. x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top; arm bases at y = +305 and -305. One fixed layout.
Bench centre (concentricity tester, compact cast-iron model: bench 350 x 110, centre height 75, 200 between centres, about 8 kg, as the Helios Preisser 0780104 / Mahr 818 type) standing on the table along y: bench x 125-235, y -135 to +215, 40 tall; centre line x 180, z 115. Measuring stand removed from its T-slot. Tailstock heads 64 long x 46 wide, top z 143, a V-prism on each (to z 153), an eccentric clamp lever at each foot.
Left tailstock: fixed hardened 60-degree point, tip at y +126.1. Right tailstock, clamped for this shaft: hardened 60-degree point on a sprung sleeve sliding along y, travel 10.5; spring 4.0 N at full extension, rising 0.4 N/mm (estimate); fully out, its tip is at y -20.6.
Lever: steel arm with a black 20 mm ball knob leaving the back of the right tailstock; knob centre (166, -154.6, 103) at rest, pivot pin across x at (166, -81, 93) inside the head. Pressing the knob down turns the lever to its stop (28.5 degrees, knob 36 mm lower); a finger on the lever bears on a lug on the sleeve and draws it back, 10.0 at the stop. Knob force about 1.5 N at the start and 2.9 N at the stop (estimates). The finger only pulls: the work can also push the sleeve back. A return spring lifts the lever when let go.
Shaft: ground C45 steel test shaft, 16.0 across, 160 long, 0.252 kg; both ends centre-drilled DIN 332-1 B 3.15 x 6.7 (60-degree seat 6.7 across inside a 120-degree protecting chamfer 10.0 across; pilot 3.15, 7.0 deep). Mounted it spans y +132 to -28: each tip bears on its seat 5.9 inside the end face, and the sleeve sits 1.5 back from full extension, pressing about 4.6 N. With the lever on its stop the sprung tip is 2.6 clear of the shaft's right end face, so the shaft goes in one end first, turned, and swings into line.
Start: the shaft lies along y in two black-oxide steel V-blocks (50 wide x 40 long x 40 tall, 90-degree V 40 across), x 55-105, y -18 to +22 and +82 to +122; its middle at (80, +52), axis at z 31.3. Lever at rest, sprung point fully out, both grippers open at the ready pose.
Friction (estimates): steel on the hardened points 0.15, steel on the V-blocks 0.20.
scoring:
Measured at the end. A point is in its seat when its tip is within 1.0 mm of the shaft's axis and 5.0-6.8 mm inside an end face (on the chamfer a tip is at least 3.3 mm off the axis and under 1 mm in; real trial: the shaft turns freely by hand without knocking, and a close photo shows the point in the seat). A point bears on an end when its tip is within 8 mm of the axis and touches the end face or the hole but is not in its seat. Lever at rest: knob within 2 mm of its rest height. Hands off: both grippers at least 30 mm from the shaft and from the knob. Still: over 1 s the shaft moves under 0.5 mm and its axis turns under 0.5 degree (turning about its own axis, which centres allow, does not count).
1.0: a point in its seat at each end, lever at rest, hands off, still for 1 s.
0.75: a point in its seat at each end and the shaft still, but a gripper within 30 mm of the shaft or the knob, or the lever not at rest.
0.5: one point in its seat and the other bearing on the other end's chamfer or face instead of its seat, hands off and still (a false-runout mount).
0.25: one point in its seat, otherwise (for example the free end still held).
0: anything else, including the shaft still in its V-blocks.
Sticky 0 for the rest of the run: the shaft ever lies on the table or on the bench's top, or leaves the table.
Forcing cap: the sprung centre is to be drawn back by its lever. If the work ever pushes the sleeve more than 3 mm back from where it last stood while the lever's finger is not on it (the shaft rammed against the point, which marks the centre hole), the run scores at most 0.5. Video shows lever and sleeve together.
reset_notes: Hold the lever down, lift the shaft off and lay it back in its V-blocks with its middle at the mark; let the lever up. Wipe both points and both centre holes with a clean cloth. Replace the shaft if it was dropped or a centre hole is marked. Bench and V-blocks stay in place; the tailstock stays clamped.
fidelity: Rigid bodies. The sprung centre is a slide joint with a linear spring (4.0 N preload, 0.4 N/mm); the lever is a hinge with a return spring whose finger bears on a lug on the sleeve, so it only pulls. Each centre hole is 16 convex sectors (60- and 120-degree cones, pilot hole); the points are convex 60-degree cones. Spring, lever ratio and knob position are estimates to measure on the real bench centre. No dial indicator is fitted; the runout reading is not scored.
